utterances.text: I don't have knowledge of this attack in Here on the 21st of March, but perhaps the attack in Konjic on the 23rd -- perhaps we can view that through a different context, in a different context, where a little while before that, both for the military and civilian authorities, Safet Cibo was appointed for Konjic, Jablanica, and Prozor, and he addressed the population over Radio Konjic, and then Croats could not have any access to Konjic anymore. So propaganda again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's look at paragraph 5(b) of this report, which is a report from SpaBat Sector, and paragraph 5(b) relates to Konjic. It says: "According to Slobodan Bobic (HVO vice-defence minister), on March 24th, Muslim elements killed two Croats, wounded eight more, and arrested a further 22 of the HVO." And it goes on: "The situation abated somewhat when Bruno Stojic and Brigadier Petkovic visited the area and organised the release of the detainees. The comment is this activity was a consequence rather than a cause of the tension which has been increasing in the Konjic-Jablanica area during the past week. The heightened state of tension was demonstrated by the significant increase in the number of check-points in town as well as an increase in the manning of these check-points." Sir, it seems that the internationals viewed that the events in Konjic, that attack on the 23rd and then -- which was then stopped by Petkovic and Stojic a day later, it seems that that attack was not -- should not be viewed only in the context of Konjic, you can't view it in isolation. You need to look at the broader context. That activity was a consequence rather than a cause of the tension; isn't that so? Konjic you can't view in isolation; you have to view it in the broader context of the region. What happened in Jablanica and Prozor would also impact.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at 5(b), referring to Konjic, you will see that an additional 22 HVO members were arrested, which means that prior to that there were 150 HVO members arrested, as had been admitted by the ABiH, and that the attack was going on across the area. On the 23rd, an agreement was signed by the HVO and the ABiH in order to put a stop to that conflict. And as I've already said it, after that the scale of the conflict was first reduced and then the scale -- the conflict was stopped, but a big contribution towards that was a very bad weather. You can see that the report is not comprehensive and that the number of 150 is not mentioned. We see that there is a reference to the 21st, but whereas the 23rd the report is not comprehensive, which may be due to the fact that it was not easy to come by information at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next month, April. Now, sir, with regard to the events in April in the municipality of Jablanica, your testimony was: "To the best of my knowledge, the HVO had never planned that." And that was on the 19th of January at transcript reference 48654 [realtime transcript read in error "48694"], line 20. Sir, by that do you mean that the HVO did not attack in Jablanica in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, the HVO didn't launch any attacks on the town of Jablanica. What the HVO did was to try and help the Croats who were completely encircled there. That was an active defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You are aware of the ultimatum -- the April ultimatum by the HVO to the ABiH in April, issued on the 5th of April, to expire on the 15th of April? Are you aware of that ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's look at paragraph 18 -- Exhibit P01808. It's just the next document in your binder. Exhibit P01808. This is in evidence. Sir, this is a media report published in "Borba" on the 5th of April, 1993, and we've provided in your binder an enlarged version of it to make it easier for you to read. You'll see that there's a photograph on the top right-hand side of the picture, and just beneath that photograph there's an article entitled "HVO Ultimativno Trazi." You see that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This article says -- it's about the HVO ultimatum: "HVO ultimatum demands pullout of Muslim troops from three provinces: "Zagreb. The Croatian Defence Council yesterday called for the pullout of Muslim troops from the provinces assigned to the Croats under a UN peace plan, thus heightening the tensions between the nominal allies. "The HVO command set April 15 as the dead-line for Alija Izetbegovic to sign a joint document which calls for a pullout of troops and the creation of a joint command, thus confirming that there are no disagreements between Croats and Muslims." Sir, do you have no knowledge of this?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of the ultimatum. However, another reference is made to provinces. That was in April, and as far as I know the Vance-Owen Plan was signed in March and included the proposals by both the Croatian and Muslim sides. I don't see where the problem lies. I don't know about any ultimatums.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's read the next paragraph: "'If Izetbegovic does not sign the agreement by 15 April, the HVO will unilaterally establish its authority in Provinces 3, 8 and 10,' says a communique from the HVO General Staff in Mostar." That's a reference to the Main Staff where you were working. They issued this communique. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the fifth time, perhaps, I will have the following objection to a similar question. We have already spoken at great length about the text in "Borba" and in Reuters, and we had Veso Vegar as a witness in this courtroom, and I believe that it was established in this court that no information was issued by the Main Staff of the HVO. Could that please be borne in mind, rather to use a newspaper text from the Belgrade-based "Borba," and ask the witness about something that he could not have any knowledge about and that has been proven in this courtroom as not being the truth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, the Defence is saying that the Main Staff never issued any press releases and that one needs to be wary of this article published in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, a small correction, but it makes life easier later, but the -- I was trying to find the reference at page 49, line 20 of today's transcript to the 19th of January, given as 48694. It's actually 48654. It's probably worth noting, because later we'll look for it and it's not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Your Honour. It is, indeed, as Mr. Stewart spoke. I misspoke on that, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Maybe not to forget later, the previous discussion of my dear colleague Mr. Stewart is recorded as Mr. Kruger is speaking, so later we would forget who is speaking what.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I suppose I should also point out that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I should also point out that if the corrected references that I've just given don't then appear correctly on the transcript now, nothing is achieved. And a few lines back, it's given as "4655." What did I say, "48654," I think is what I said. Mr. Kruger can confirm that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's wrong again. You said "48654," not "46," I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now I've got it, thank you. Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I did -- as I sat down, same old problem. Once it happens once, it carries on happening, doesn't it? That's a rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, you were in the Main Staff during April 1993. Was there any talk that you were aware of in the Main Staff about an ultimatum and a dead-line of 15 April?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of any ultimatums.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the next document in the binder, which is P01872. And we won't dwell upon this document. We'll just quickly look at it. It's an order from Miljenko Lasic of the 14th of April, 1993. It's an HVO order. It says: "In view of carrying out the combat mission in the Prozor-Jablanica area, I order:" And then follows what he orders. Now, sir, you'd agree that this is very clearly a combat -- an order preparing the HVO for combat missions? You don't disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at the date, which is the 14th of April, and Miljenko Lasic's order, we will see that that was a reaction to the activities previously undertaken by the BiH Army. This is what I have already been talking about. That was when artillery support was requested for Boksevica and for the areas penetrated by their sabotage forces. If we look at the artillery of the Operations Zone South-East Herzegovina and North-West Herzegovina, in my view, the only logical explanation would be that that was that artillery support. It was not previously planned. It was a reaction to something that had happened, and an order was then issued to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, you've given a long explanation, but you still haven't answered the question. You don't disagree that this is clearly an order for combat missions by the HVO, regarding combat missions for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely agree, and I would say that this was a combat mission, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's go three documents further in your binder, and this is document P01915, P01915. Now, this is an interim report two days later. It's dated the 16th of April, 1993, and it's by Colonel Zeljko Siljeg. And if we note the addressees, it's to the Department of Defence in Mostar and to the Main Staff of the HVO. Now, if we go to paragraph 7 and paragraph 8 of this report, it says: "Co-ordinating with Tuta is done through the Posusje unit of Sovicka." And 8: "Beginning of today's operation on selected targets, next to the village of Slatina at 7.00 and on the village of Sovici from 9.00." Now, sir, my question to you is: This appears to be very close to an attack order. Isn't this an attack order regarding the village of Sovici?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a combat or, rather, an attack order. I need to read the whole document, but I can tell you that this is a report from a commander who had his zone of responsibility, and he submitted a report. For me to be able to comment upon this document, I have to read the entire report to be able to tell you what's herein. So this is not an order. This a report, reporting about the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And according to what you see there in this report, what is being reported is that Sovici is going to be attacked at 9.00?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it says "Selectively on military targets." That's how I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Have a look at paragraph 13, the very last item of the document. It says: "We continue to work according to plan." Now, sir, do you allow that there was actually a plan being implemented in this area by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it says, looking at bullet point 1: "In the command of the Rama Brigade, we are establishing a forward command post." This a plan to establish a forward command post in order to be able to resist attacks which were mounting in the area. When you want to establish a forward command post, it takes some time. In other words, this is a plan to establish a forward command post in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Doesn't this refer to all the previous points in this document, 1 to 12, and it says, We have reported to you and it's all according to the plan? Isn't that what this says?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report by a commander. What exactly did he have in mind? There's no way for me to know. But I believe that he was talking about his plan to establish a forward command post as a reaction to what had happened previously in the area. We see the date 16 April, and we know that the intense activities started on the 13th of April. In my view, as an analyst, I would say that I am right in interpreting the commander's words, but what he really meant is a different story.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, as an analyst, you see that this report was addressed to, inter alia, Mr. Stojic, and it was addressed to the chief of the Main Staff, General Petkovic. Now, certainly Colonel Siljeg, when he wrote this, it's safe to assume that when he refers to "the plan" or "this plan," that Mr. Stojic and General Petkovic would know what he was talking about. As an analyst, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an analyst, looking back at that time, I can say that Mr. Stojic and everybody else got very much involved with a view to pacifying the situation. It was common knowledge that there was a lot going on, and you can see that something was done in order to prevent further attacks against the units of the HVO which were deployed in the area -- in the enclaves around Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I allowed the witness to provide his answer, but I have to object. The document doesn't say that it was ever sent to Mr. Stojic. It was sent to the Defence Department. We have had documents which expressly refer to Mr. Stojic. This is not one of them. And I just wanted to be very precise in that respect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this is an important document in light of the indictment; namely, as regards Sovici and Doljani. The case put by the Prosecution is that the HVO attacked, together with Tuta's unit, and with a number of consequences. I'm looking at this document as it stands in front of us. There is something at the end which mentions a plan. In your language, "planu," "po planu." A Judge that only reads this document can infer that an offensive is being launched, but this would not take into account what happened on the 13th, 14th, and 15th of April. And you addressed this very briefly, and we've seen documents relating to that. Since you were a member of the Main Staff at the time, since you were an analyst, as far as you remember - it is very difficult to remember everything after such a long time when so much happened, it's difficult perhaps to jolt your memory - but at the time, as far as you remember, did the HVO react after there had been an attack by the ABiH or did the HVO launch an attack, which is not the same thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The HVO absolutely reacted to an attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this document, if I analyse it without taking into account what happened on the 13th, 14th, and 15th of April, for which we have a great number of documents, there's a small technical point of detail which caught my attention, and that has to do with the radio connections and the fact that it was important to install a mobile repeater coming from Tomislavgrad. Do you see what I mean? It's mentioned here. After the list of artillery pieces, 1, 2, 3, and then there is a need to install that; i.e., it is important to have four Motorolas. If there is such a plan as put forward by the Prosecution, I wonder why this hadn't been planned beforehand, to install the entire communications system. This is clearly done in a hurry and there's nothing there, so it has to be brought in from Tomislavgrad. Either they are totally incompetent, which could well be the case, or this small technical detail indicates that the HVO was faced with an offensive and they had to prepare for a counter-offensive by installing an adequate communications system which wasn't working properly. I don't know exactly what your knowledge of military affairs are. I know that you went to military school, I know that you're an officer, but I don't know if you're currently involved in a number of operations conducted by NATO, with the participation of the Croatian forces. I don't know. But when there is a plan, in technical terms, are the communications systems not a priority when such a plan exists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, absolutely, communications are a priority, and you can see that there was no plan in place. If there had been a plan, then we, as the military intelligence, would have had to provide elements for such a plan, and I know that we have never provided such elements. And you can see here that this was organised as a reaction to something and that we were taken by surprise. A repeater was then brought in and set up in order to establish communication among the different elements of the artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have just mentioned a detail which is important. This could be drowned in what you are saying. You are saying that if there was a plan, the VOS would have been involved beforehand, upstream, not at the last minute. As far as you remember, while you worked as an analyst, do you have any memory of a plan that would have been prepared beforehand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only plan that had been prepared and that I'm aware of at the level of the Main Staff was Operation Tempest in the month of November, 1992, against the VRS, and the Military Intelligence was a part of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are saying that this famous Bura Operation which we have heard a great deal about, well, that you were involved in that. To conclude, if a large-scale operation in Sovici-Doljani had been prepared, you should have been involved, and you are saying this under oath. You are saying that you were not involved, We were not involved, so there's no plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, I was not involved, there was no plan in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the record, on page 59, line 2, the witness said "Operation Bura." We have spoken about Operation Bura on a number of occasions. Maybe we should stick to the Croatian word rather than attempt to translate it into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, let's then look at another document, P01936. It's the very next document in your binder, P01936, and this is another interim report by Colonel Siljeg on the 17th of April, 1993, addressed to the Main Staff of the Croatian Defence Council in Mostar and the Operative Zone North-West Herzegovina, Tomislavgrad: "Interim report for the situation at 0900 hours." And then he says: "This morning at 6.00, we began to implement the plan." So, sir, there was a plan?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A plan? Well, it might just be the word used, "plan," plan to help people under siege in the Konjic region, used that way. But there wasn't a written plan as something that is elaborated for anything like that. It's just a plan to assist those people who are in jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: But you're just speculating on that, because you don't really know, do you?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that at the level of the Main Staff, there was no plan. So the word "plan," well, you can say -- we used to say, We're working according to plan, but there was no actual plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Now, sir, just further on how the ABiH was viewing or interpreting what they saw coming from the HVO side, let's look at document P11078.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second. Witness, the word "plan" is important, because there are two versions, there are two cases. The Prosecutor argues that there was a plan, and you are saying that there was no plan, and Judges will have to rule on this. I see in the B/C/S version the word "plana" or "plan," and I see that it's a report from the 17th of April to the Main Staff and it's coming from Mr. Siljeg. So it's coming from -- it's going to the top. And Colonel Siljeg is reporting to the Main Staff, so going upstream, probably saying to General Petkovic that, We started at 6.00 a.m. and we began to implement the plan. And he points out that the operations are going to go towards the villages of the Prozor municipality, and he gives a list. This is what is puzzling, because you say that you had maps, you had other documents, and you would jot down everything that was happening. So if you are -- if what you're saying is true, in theory, this report sent to General Petkovic would be sent to the VOS or to the officer in charge, and on your map you are going to put arrows like "Gorica," "Paros," "Parcani," and so on, stating that some actions will be taken there. So as far as you can recollect, were you given this document on the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document -- well, I don't remember this document, I don't remember having been given it. We received from this zone -- from VOS, V-O-S, down our chain of information, but this obviously went down the chain of command, whereas from VOS, of the operations zone we would receive, on a regular basis, information and reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not trying to speculate, but from a military point of view, 13th, 14th, and 15th of April, the ABiH is launching an attack. The HVO shows some resistance and launches a counter-attack. Colonel Siljeg, from his forward command post because he is apparently in Prozor, is in touch via radio communication with General Petkovic, and minute after minute he keeps him posted. And on the 16th of April, either by radio communication or by telephone, they set up the counter-offensive. And on the 16th of April, Colonel Siljeg says to him, Tomorrow morning at 6.00 a.m., I will launch my attack on all those small villages, and we are going to take part, and that is Parcani, Visnjani, and so on and so forth. General Petkovic says, That's well and good. Go ahead. And on the 17th of April at 9.00 a.m., which means three hours later, he reports that according to the plan, this is what happened. From a military point of view, could this be a proper sequence of events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm looking at the axis of action, Slatina mentioned here. As far as I'm concerned, it would only -- the only logical thing would be to alleviate the Boksevica and Neretva River Valley area [as interpreted], where the HVO were in a very difficult position, so to reinforce them. That is the only logical thing, that it went along that way. So in conformity with the assistance they had asked for previously both from the Operations Zone South-East Herzegovina and North-West Herzegovina, and where proposals were made about the pressure from the north, all I can see here is a request to help the area out because the units were far -- had far less manpower -- the HVO had far less manpower and, as such, they found it difficult to survive and to maintain the areas they controlled. So this is by way of alleviating the situation in those areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a correction to the transcript. In line 8, it was recorded as being the Neretva River Valley area. The witness said "Neretvica."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Neretvica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because they are two different rivers; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So according to you, this plan, what was its purpose? Was it to lift some pressure off, because the ABiH was putting pressure on the Neretvica region and attacking those villages would lift some pressure off this region? Is that what the plan was all about? Is that what you're trying to say here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think there was any plan. It was just assistance, reaction to the existing situation, and that they wanted to lift the burden over the units in the Konjic and Jablanica area that were in a difficult position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to skip a few documents. I'm going to refer you to Exhibit P01949. 1949. This exhibit is already in evidence. Now, sir, this is still the same period, and this is the 18th of April, and it's an order for further action by Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic, and it's addressed to, inter alia, Prozor, Siljeg, and it says: "1. Urgently reinforce the troops that are carrying out offensive operations towards Klis." So, sir, from this it's correct that the HVO was actually in an attack mode, this time in Klis?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here: "Urgently reinforce the forces carrying out offensive operations towards Klis." So that's precisely what I was saying, towards Neretvica. So obviously the forces who -- which wanted to assist the area did not succeed and that they needed to be reinforced to lift the burden off Klis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: But, sir, the question is: From 1 it's clear that the HVO is carrying out offensive operations, it's attacking towards Klis. Isn't that exactly what it says here?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This part of the order being mentioned and what we have on the ground, you should view this integrally, comprehensively, and we can call it exclusively "active defence." So there are some elements of attack, but exclusively to gain a better defence position and not to take control of something, so that the defence could be put into a better position so as to be able to resist enemy attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Paragraph 2: "You should assess whether you have forces available for attack on Here, Kute, and Scipe." That's clearly contemplating attack?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at this here, Here, Kute, Scipe, it's an area north-west of the Neretvica Valley, along the Neretvica Valley. Now, from where the attacks came along the Neretvica Valley and further on towards the municipalities of Prozor and Vakuf. Now, they are Muslim villages from which units arrived which attack this area. So here, too -- now, Slatina is the lower side, southerly. This is northerly. So they wanted to lift the burden of this entire siege. So in geographic terms, it's one area which belongs to different municipalities, but it's one general region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, paragraph 4: "Zeljko, I hope you understand the order." Do you have any idea what General Petkovic means when he says this? Is he giving a coded message to Zeljko Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what coded thing this could be, except to be understood just how important the area was. So unless assistance is given, there wouldn't be any more HVO units there. It would have been completely militarily routed. I don't know what else this could mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, before completing this topic, let's have one more look at the ECMM report which we looked at earlier today. This is P02430.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would like to ask the witness about the following in connection with the number 4 question, which says that: "Zeljko, I hope you understand the order." And in this connection, I would like to ask Mr. Jasak about the following: If in number 1 and 2 there are references to reinforce the troops that are carrying out offensive operations, then: "You should assess whether you have forces available for attack on Here, Kute, and Scipe." Then would you find any contradiction with number 3, paragraph number 3 of the order, which says that: "In accordance with the order to cease the hostilities, I will meet with Halilovic tomorrow and UNPROFOR will have the role of a mediator"? So my question is that although in numbers 1 and 2 there are a clear reference as far as the offensive operations, in number 3 there is information that there will be talks about a cease-fire, in that context what is your position on this order? And then probably you can reconsider your previous answer about paragraph number 4, if it is coded or not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I tried to analyse this as a soldier. We have units that are under siege, in an encirclement. The only way to try, from various axes, to attack -- the only way in which we can lift the burden off these units, we had information that the BH Army was attacking -- was on the attack, regardless of the fact that on the 18th an agreement was signed, and we could see from their orders that they had no intention of respecting it. So here I think that General Petkovic has attempted, by issuing this order, to act and to ensure that his meeting with General Halilovic does not result in a complete military routing of the HVO, because then they would have nothing to discuss. That's how I understand this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Are you saying, Mr. Jasak, that this is an order to implement a cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. After this, the 24th [as interpreted] in Zenica, they agreed on a cease-fire; Generals Petkovic and Halilovic, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the operations continued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, might I correct the transcript. In line 19, what was recorded is the witness having said "the 24th in Zenica." The witness said "the 20th of April," "the 20th of April."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, the document we have is an important exhibit from the Prosecution, and it may be used in their final submission as to what happened. Therefore, we have to look at this document in detail. There are four paragraphs, and they have to be linked to each other when read. It seems that there is some sort of a code here. When General Petkovic is sending this document to Colonel Siljeg, it is encrypted, so it's confidential. Point 1, it's obvious it's a surprise attack. We are not aware of all the situation and we don't know what was the position of the HVO and the ABiH in Klis, but you say that the situation was difficult. As for point 2, as for Here, Kute and Scipe, it is obviously not an attack. They have to first assess whether they have the forces available. So this document is mainly targeting Klis. Then we move to points 3 and 4, and here you have to really read it carefully. At first glance, I see that in an official military document, General Petkovic calls Siljeg by his first name, Zeljko. I don't know whether he's saying the formal "you" or the informal "you," but it's: "I hope you understand the order." But is this referring to number 1 or to number 3? If it's referring to 1, it's very clear, they have to do their utmost for this operation. But if it's linked to number 3, then we are buying into the case of the Prosecution, which could be the following: In Bosnia-Herzegovina during this period, there was some hostilities and there was some cease-fires. Here, General Petkovic knows that. The following day, he will meet with Halilovic, and that UNPROFOR is going to play its role. And as a result of this meeting, there will be a cease-fire. It's obvious. And he is trying to explain to Zeljko that since there's going to be a cease-fire, they have to win immediately. So in military terms, it could mean that you have to win this position immediately, and he's basically saying to him, I hope you understand, because as early as the 19th of April, the following day, UNPROFOR will blow the whistle and will say that it's the end of the game. So he's pre-empting this. So according to you, is point 4 to be read with a link to number 3 or to number 1, if you have any knowledge as a military analyst? If you don't know anything, you can say so and we can move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it refers to point 1. I don't know in what context. It could relate to the rest, but the most -- essential point is that we can see here the forces acting towards Klis, so if they are not being effective, they need to be reinforced. And to lift the burden, it says in point 2, You should assess whether you have forces available. I think that's what that refers to. And point 3 would simply be that they should try and see that the villages -- these villages don't fall until some agreement is reached, well, in military terms. That's my interpretation of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, please look at me rather than looking either to your left or to your right. The situation in Klis, what happened? Did the BiH attack? What really happened in Klis, because I'm not aware of anything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Klis, they were under siege. The BH Army was attacking parts of the HVO in the Neretvica River Valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the HVO is surrounded in Klis; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The HVO was encircled mostly throughout the area of the Konjic municipality. There were enclaves that existed, and it was in a very disadvantageous position, the HVO, and so, in my view, all this was planned to make it be in a better position to avoid failure, militarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Kruger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I'm not going to show you any further documents from this binder. I'll just ask you one final question to wrap up. Sir, from your testimony on various documents that I've shown you, your testimony has essentially been that where the international observers have come to the conclusion, probably based on their intelligence or the intelligence available to them, that the HVO was actually principally the party provoking conflict in the Konjic-Jablanica area in 1993, are they wrong when they come to those conclusions?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not claiming that they are setting out untruthful data, but quite simply that information after the 13th of April, 1993, that information could not have arrived, because they couldn't enter Croatian enclaves. That was not permitted. They weren't able to see the consequences of the actions of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I propose stepping on to topics in binder 3, but perhaps this may be a time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, it's probably better to have a break before we move to binder number 3. We'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Kruger, you have two hours and eight minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jasak, I'd now like to turn to Mostar, and the first thing I'd like to refer you to or ask you about is: On the 20th of January last week, you testified, and I'll get the -- try and get the reference right this time, at transcript reference 48681, and from line 10 this is the question: "Mr. Jasak, in this courtroom we saw evidence that the vast majority of these people were of Muslim ethnicity." Now, this is talking about the people who were detained at Velez Stadium on the 9th of May, 1993, and then taken to Heliodrom: "Could you explain to us why there was such a disproportionately large number of Muslims among these people, compared to the composition of the population at that point in time?" And, sorry, sir, I'm not referring to a document, so you needn't look for a document. I'm reading from your own testimony. Your answer to this question was: "Well, I'll try. In my opinion, the only possible explanation is that a large number of Croats had already moved out of that part of town. They had taken their children to continue their schooling elsewhere. And a large part of the inhabitants of Mostar came from the surrounding municipalities, and they may have gone away for the weekend. Also, when people heard shells falling, they left the town in their own vehicles." Sir, from this response of yours, are you telling the Court that the ethnicity of those arrested in Mostar on the 9th of May, 1993, was totally coincidental?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, an objection to the use of the verb "arrest."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, are you telling the Court that the ethnicity of all those people detained in Mostar on the 9th of May, 1993, was totally coincidental?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any other explanation, save for what I have already said in the course of my testimony. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Is it correct that 10 days later, General Petkovic was negotiating about the release of these Muslims who were held at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the VOS is concerned, the VOS was not involved in any negotiations at all. But I know that there were talks about releasing all detainees kept both by the BiH Army and the HVO. It would have been an exchange, all for all. That was all I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I deliberately allowed the witness to answer. I would just like to remind everybody that under the indictment, people who were detained at the Heliodrom on the 9th of May were released within approximately eight days. So their release could not have been negotiated after 10 days because they had already been released.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's move on. Have a look at the very last document in your binder, and that is a Defence exhibit that was shown to you last week. It's Exhibit 4D01344.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Kruger, but I believe at least in my binder, the last one is 1242.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour. We're moving to binder 3. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: My apology for not making that clear. Binder 3, the very last document is 4D01344.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, you remember this document? This the document showing an agreement between General Mladic and General Halilovic, brokered by Philippe Morillon on the 8th of May, 1993, the cease-fire agreement. You recall this?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, just to refresh your memory, you were shown the document and you were asked to interpret what the document showed regarding the Muslims, and this is on the 20th of January, 2010; transcript reference 48675 -- sorry, 48676 from line 5. You said: "I would interpret this document in the following way: that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina no longer intended to fight the Army of Republika Srpska and that they were turning to the creation of their own living environment, at the detriment of their hitherto ally, that is to say, the Croats." You remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And you also stated that you had information that since January, the Muslims and the Serbs were negotiating with each other or talking to each other; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You told General Petkovic about this?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: VOS, well, about the knowledge that there were talks, we came to that information and we sent it on further. The VOS, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And this agreement on the 8th of May, 1993, was information on this also forwarded to General Petkovic by VOS?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was common knowledge, because it concerned UNPROFOR representatives and it was generally known that they were negotiating. But apart from this, some other talks were held that we knew about at that time, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you are aware of the fact that shortly after this, General Petkovic and General Mladic, they also met under the auspices of General Morillon, and Muslims were not present at that occasion? You were aware that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If I tell you that on the 16th of May, 1993, there was, indeed, such a meeting, would that change your assessment that it's inappropriate for the Serbs and the Muslims to meet, with no Croats being present?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wouldn't change it, because after these meetings there were some other meetings, and they were talks about demilitarisation, for instance, of the enclaves in Eastern Bosnia, and the BH Army units would pull out of Central Bosnia, because it was about demilitarisation of Sarajevo as well, where a large number of soldiers would pull out to the area of Central Bosnia. And that's what prompted us to see this agreement as problematic because it would have large forces from North Herzegovina, and this went along the lines of having an area void of Croats or the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at the document, you'll see that there's no signature that appears. Do you know whether this agreement was, in actual fact, signed?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We know that the talks were held, and this was indicative, as far as we were concerned, for assessing co-operation between the BH Army and the Army of Republika Srpska, that is, and for later activities which stemmed from that. And we had information and knowledge that they were working against the Croatian Defence Council, so this was confirmation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And so you did see this document at that stage; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying I saw the document, but that we knew about the talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This document here, do you know whether this is the whole agreement that was concluded or not?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was the whole agreement that was concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, if I show you a different part or even the rest of this agreement, or the documents which form this exhibit or which form the totality of the agreement, then you would have to reassess this document in the context of all those documents; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Kruger, I find that a difficult question. How can the witness say something? He doesn't know what the other documents are. All he can answer is, Perhaps. And I can answer for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I will show him the document, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's look at the totality of this document. And if you turn to just the previous document in your binder, this is Exhibit P11192, P11192.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, for the record, if I may point out that the English version of the document which forms this exhibit consisted of a number of pages in English and then one page in B/C/S. And if we look at the translation, this was drawn from the EDS, and it contains the document that was shown to the witness as 4D01344, but that entire document on EDS consists of a number of pages of B/C/S and then one page of English. For convenience, we have switched that single page of English and single page of B/C/S so that one can look at the entire English version and the entire B/C/S version without having to flip between the two versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, looking at this document, the first page, if you just look at the English version perhaps for a moment, the first page is an agreement which is signed by various persons. Now, you may not be able to read the English, but I put it to you that that is actually the signed version of the document that we were discussing just before this, 4D01344. This is the cease-fire agreement: "Cease all armed attacks or any hostile acts within the whole territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina." That's the 8th of May, 1993. But, sir, if we turn the page and we look at the next page, we see that this is actually part -- or was concluded at the same time as the agreement on the demilitarisation of Srebrenica and Zepa concluded between General Ratko Mladic and General Sefer Halilovic on 8 May, 1993. And if we actually look at section 1, the demilitarised zone is: "To demilitarise the areas of Srebrenica and Zepa." Now, sir, in that area of Srebrenica and Zepa, the HVO was not really involved in that area as a party to that conflict; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, therefore, if you look at General Mladic and General Halilovic meeting to actually deal with the conflict in Srebrenica and Zepa, this actually is of little concern to the HVO. They had no reason for being present at that meeting; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned that within the context of later on, wherein it came to the demilitarisation of Sarajevo, where the HVO did have interest. So I'm talking about the overall activities about which we had knowledge that they were ongoing. So we knew that this was going on in Eastern Bosnia, these enclaves, and that according to an agreement, they would be able to move to an area of their desire on the basis of an egress. Also, that the demilitarisation of Sarajevo would move and transfer the army to where they wanted to go. So as far as we were concerned, that was indicative; that is to say, that the BH Army was giving up the eastern part, but at all cost wished to do in Central Bosnia something that was not good for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: But, sir, your response last week was: "I would interpret this document ..." And that's only the first page of the document. If you look at the further pages of the document, that certainly must change your categorical assessment that the ABiH no longer -- was actually abandoning the HVO. We don't see that from this agreement, do we?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we take this agreement and what I've just mentioned, the fact that I knew about Sarajevo, and if we look at the activities that took place afterwards and where the artillery did open fire at HVO units, then I think that what I said yesterday is absolutely fine and stands, because I answered yesterday based on our knowledge, the information we had, that something was being discussed, and the topics. So now that you've shown me this document that I've never seen before, that it's about Eastern Bosnia, I mentioned that before you had put this document to me. So a large number of soldiers were to be pulled out to the area of Central Bosnia, so we saw that as a danger for the disappearance of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you look at the final page of the document, it's a joint statement issued by General Mladic and General Halilovic, signed -- or witnessed by General Morillon. And, of course, it informs in the first paragraph about the agreement, but if we look at paragraph 3, that's what I'd like to ask you about: "We are informing the domestic and international public that we shall be making further efforts," et cetera. Now, sir, this appears to be a press release. Is it correct that this meeting between General Mladic and General Halilovic, that wasn't a secret thing? It was being conducted openly and in full view also of the HVO; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what excerpt you're referring to. I haven't been able to locate that passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The last page of the document, it's a joint statement, and the third paragraph of that one, it says: "We are informing the domestic and international public ..." So the question is: This meeting between Mladic and Halilovic, it wasn't being conducted in secret? It was an open affair. Everybody knew about it, the HVO as well. It wasn't hidden?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said it was generally known and under the auspices of the international community, but the meetings and agreements reached apart from this, according to our information, indicated what I have told you about, because if military-able men were pulled out of this general area to Central Bosnia, then as far as we were concerned, it was a problem, we had a problem, and that was the result of this meeting -- of this agreement. So we are now assessing what the consequences were, that's what we did, and we saw a danger there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, let's just quickly turn to something else, then, regarding the 9 May events in Mostar. That involved --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Colonel, I have a follow-up question in connection with this document which we have seen already. There is an agreement between Mladic and Halilovic, under the auspices of the international community. As the document states, it applies to the entire Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I emphasise the entire country of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including Mostar. What can emerge from this? The document states that there is a cease-fire at 12.00 on the 9th of May. We see that this document considers two specific situations. One is Srebrenica; the other one is Zepa. But Sarajevo, strangely enough, is not mentioned. I don't know whether, on the 9th of May, at one minute past 12.00, no shots were fired anymore in Sarajevo. I don't know. I will check this out later. There are two possibilities. The first one is that you, the HVO, you are aware of this agreement. And you answered Mr. Kruger's question by saying, We knew about it. In that case, a new situation emerges. You were side by side with the ABiH, and behind your back the ABiH signs a pact with the VRS. Therefore, you risk having to confront two enemies, the Serbs and the Muslims. As your intelligence service operates extremely well, you realise that this agreement is going to enter into force at 12.00, and that is why the HVO attacks the Main Staff of the 4th Corps in Mostar. That is one possibility. The second possibility is that the ABiH and the Serbs agree to stop. Then the ABiH knows that as far as Mostar is concerned, the Serbs will not fire any shots at them. They know that at 12.00 sharp, there will be no more shots fired by the Serbs on Mostar. But the ABiH has a bit of a problem, because the international community, via General Morillon, are involved in this, and there is no question of deceiving him. The ABiH then, in light of the timing, attacks in the morning, since the cease-fire should only enter into force at 12.00, and they attack at 5.00 or 6.00 in the morning. Like that, General Morillon cannot turn around and say, You've deceived me. This document can be construed in different ways. What I would like to know is this: The VOS, with its telephone tapping systems, via its liaison officers which the HVO had and who were working with UNPROFOR, knew that this agreement was going to be signed and that this was going to enter into force on the 9th of May, 1993. What I would like to know is whether you knew about this for sure, or were these only rumours and, in fact, you know nothing about it? Let me add, if you knew about it, in light of the new political situation which was about to emerge after this agreement, Mr. Mate Boban must have certainly received the information, who would have then got together with Izetbegovic, Tudjman, and Morillon, Vance-Owen -- Cyril Vance and Lord Owen, and so on. We haven't seen a single document from Mate Boban concerning this agreement. There might be such a document, but we don't have an exhibit to that effect. Had you known about this, the information should have reached Mate Boban, and in that case something must have existed. When you say that you knew, are you saying this because these were rumours, or are you saying it because you knew it and you knew for sure that this was the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We knew for certain that that would happen. And I'd also like to mention the part relating to Sarajevo. So that would be a lesser problem for us, because there was no HVO in Eastern Bosnia. But when you discuss the demilitarisation of Sarajevo, without an HVO representative in Sarajevo, then that is a problem and was a problem for us. And that kind of thing would be contained in our reports. So a couple of days after this, I think that in one of our reports the demilitarisation of Sarajevo is expressly mentioned, and the talks held on that topic. So as far as we were concerned, it was a problem for us, the arrival of a large number of soldiers, which we expected, as a result of these agreements into Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just inquire about something? I don't wish to disrupt the course of the evidence, but at page 79, I've got line 23, but it may be line 20, Your Honour said: "I don't know whether on the 9th of May, at one minute past 12.00, no shots were fired anymore in Sarajevo. I don't know. I will check this out later." May I just invite Your Honour, with respect, to confirm that what Your Honour has in mind is to check out in the evidence in this case. I have, actually, no recollection, I must say, whether any such point is in the evidence in this case, but I take it that is what Your Honour means, that that search will be in the evidence before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course I will check as part of what we have in this file. But as far as I know, we don't have anything, but you never know. Maybe one document would have gone astray. But this is obvious what you're saying. To go back to what the witness was saying, you say that you knew that -- know that within the HVO, that if this agreement was implemented, there would be the following consequences; namely, the arrival of new troops from the Serb side, and perhaps also from the ABiH, and this could lead to some consequences. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that from the area where demilitarisation was underway in Eastern Bosnia. So according to our knowledge, we had knowledge and information to the effect that the BH Army and the Army of Republika Srpska had reached an agreement to enable the units to leave those protected areas and go where they wanted to go, and it was our assessment that that would be Central Bosnia. So if a large number of forces from Eastern Bosnia and Sarajevo comes into Central Bosnia, it would present a major problem for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I understand what you are saying. But does that mean that from a military point of view, the HVO could say, Well, we're going to make sure that this plan fails by launching an attack on the 9th of May, in the morning? Could this not be construed as a military answer to this plan with a cease-fire between the Serbs and the ABiH? From the military point of view, don't you think that an attack would make sure that everything that was planned would fail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was absolutely no planning of an attack, no planned attack at all. And I said earlier on that had there been anything, that the VOS would have taken part in the planning of such a thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm listening to you, and you say, We knew. But does that mean that Mate Boban knew, that Mr. Prlic knew, that Mr. Stojic knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they could have known. We can assume that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At this point, Your Honour, I do object, because so far the gentleman has not mentioned Mr. Prlic and we haven't seen a single, solitary document that shows that anything came from VOS to Mr. Prlic. So I do object to hypothesising and speculating as to what Mr. Prlic might have known. If the Court wishes to pose a direct question, whether he sent any information directly to Mr. Prlic, the Court can do so. But to then speculate and throw names out there, I do object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the counsel intervened, you said that they were in a position to know. What did you mean when you said that they were in a position to know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, from the last paragraph, when it says "by this we informed the international community," I assume that they could have known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you don't know whether they got to know this, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't know whether they arrived at that information and knowledge, except for the part where I said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. As far as you can recollect --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: As far as I can see from the transcript, the witness didn't finish his answer before the next question came from Your Honour. That's what I heard on the English translation and what I see on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, I was listening to the French version and I didn't check on the English version. You didn't finish and I interrupted you. Go ahead. Could you please repeat what you just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Your Honour, because what I said is this: The information about co-operation between the BH Army and the Army of Republika Srpska was contained in our reports, those which were written in May, but after the 9th of May, after the 9th of May, so this was an important portion related to Sarajevo. So that was our focus, because it was talks -- a matter of talks without the presence of the Croats or, rather, the HVO Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This will be my last question. I did not have time to look at all the documents, and I will do this, of course, later on. But as far as you can recollect or as far as you know, on the 9th, on the 10th, and 11th of May, do you know whether the Serb artillery opened fire towards Mostar East or Mostar West? Did they start -- did they open fire or did they stop doing that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what I know, fire was opened on the HVO position -- positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Kruger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, just to finish, perhaps, on this agreement of the 8th of May, 1993, between Mladic and Halilovic, sir, is it correct that this agreement, it didn't stop the conflict between the Serbs and the Muslims? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, even after this, there were activities. I don't know whether the activities stopped at the moment when this was signed. We know only too well that there were conflicts after this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So let's turn to something else regarding Mostar, the events of the 9th of May, 1993. It's correct that on that day, there was a large-scale HVO involvement in those events; you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I know, I've already told you what I know. There was fighting around that time around the president's office, which means in the area west of the agreed line of separation which existed at the time, which points to the fact that the fighting didn't take place east of that, which means that the HVO defended itself, because near the president's office there was a parish office and the local priest was also taken away in an unknown direction, and it was only in the evening they will learn as to where he had been taken to. There were a lot of refugees who were around North Camp who had been expelled to the right bank. Fire was opened on the Tihomir Misic Barracks, Bijela Brijeg was also shelled, and this is the long and the short of what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, from the long and the short of what you know, you can perhaps answer the question: There was, indeed, large-scale HVO involvement on the 9th of May in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO was involved in defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, it's also so that on that day, the HVO displaced thousands of Muslim inhabitants to Velez, and from there to Heliodrom? You don't disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't talk about numbers, and I believe that this was not a resettlement. I believe that those people were moved from the territory affected by combat, and I really wouldn't be able to confirm that they were only Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: But they were moved by the HVO; that's correct, isn't it? That you should know.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who displaced them. Maybe they, themselves, decided to flee from the war. Maybe somebody told them where to go. I really wouldn't be able to tell you how all that came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And do you know that the people who were so displaced were taken to Heliodrom and held there for many days by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem is the word "displaced," and I think if we look at the previous answers, there seems to be -- this is a term of art which the gentleman may be aware of. I don't want to be giving any answers away, but perhaps a clearer choice of words might assist in this exchange, because "displacement" does have a particular connotation, and I believe that's what the gentleman was referring to in his previous answer. Now we're bringing "displacement" into Heliodrom. Before he was saying "arrest," then he said "detention," now it's "displacement." He should pick one and stick with the term.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, with respect, I think that everybody in the courtroom know what's being referred to, and the witness, being in Mostar, certainly knows about large numbers of Muslims [realtime transcript read in error "prisoners"] being taken to Heliodrom and being held there for various days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And I'm simply asking: You know about that, sir, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that on the evening news I learned about all that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, there seems to be a mistake in the way how Mr. Kruger's question was recorded on line 11. It says here "prisoners taken to Heliodrom," and I don't think that Mr. Kruger used the term "prisoners."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I think that's entirely correct. I think that I did refer to persons, or maybe it was Muslims, but the question remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's move on. You, yourself, also confirmed in testimony last week that the HVO attacked the ABiH in the Vranica building. You agree with that still?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that the HVO had launched an attack. There was fighting for the Vranica building, and it was a reaction to previous events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So let me read your testimony to you, and this comes from the transcript of the 19th of January, 2010, and the transcript reference is page 48674 from line 5. The question was: "Now my question, Mr. Jasak: Is it correct when it is asserted that the HVO attacked BH Army positions in the Vranica building? "A. To the best of my knowledge, this information is correct." So, sir, are you now saying that you were wrong when you said that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within a context. The entire city of Mostar came under attack, according to what I know. Fighting was taking place all over the city. The HVO opened fire on the ABiH, but in order to defend themselves, not in order to attack, to choose any part of the BiH Army as targets. That was part of defence. There was combat, but as part of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, it's actually the 20th of January. The page number is right this time, but the date is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I stand corrected. The 20th of January. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, why I'm asking you all of this is just to come to this point, and I think this is the last thing that I'll touch upon before the time runs out: On the 19th of January, last week, you were asked -- and I'll give the transcript reference first. The transcript is T-48663 from line 24. Ms. Alaburic asked you: "Let me ask you for your opinion, if you believe you know enough about what was going on at the time. Any continuation of these BH Army activities --" Just for context, we're referring here -- this was -- what was being talked about was the ABiH actions on the 25th of April, 1993, and it was alleged that they broke a cease-fire agreement: "Any continuation of these BH Army activities, which in itself flew in the face of the cease-fire that was agreed, do you think anything like that could have been possible or would have been without the consent of the high-ranking commanders in the BH Army?" And to this, your response was: "Nothing like this could have happened unbeknownst to high-ranking commanders in the BH Army. Maybe something like this could have gone on for a single day, but if anyone had failed to carry out an order actually signed by President Izetbegovic, this person would then have been removed, meaning even President Izetbegovic, himself, would have known about this, as well as their supreme military command." Sir, my question is: Given the large-scale involvement of HVO military in Mostar on the 9th of May, and in taking a number of Muslims to Velez Stadium, and taking them from there to Heliodrom and holding them there for many days, are you prepared to make the same categorical assertion with regard to the knowledge of the HVO's military leaders, that they would have known?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an entirely different matter. On the 25th of April, nothing [as interpreted] happened. And on the 18th of April, there was an agreement between Boban and Izetbegovic. On the 20th, there was an agreement between Generals Petkovic and Halilovic, which means that if things had been done after the 10th of May, I would be able to agree. If an agreement had been signed about Mostar between Izetbegovic and Boban on the 10th of May, and if we remember that that was on the 18th, and then seven days after that, on the 25th, so if this had been signed on the 10th and if the fighting had taken place on the 17th, then I would totally agree with what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a correction. Line 21, it says that the witness said "on the 25th of April, nothing happened," whereas the witness said "on the 25th of April, there was an attack." And then he explained how this transpired seven days after the cease-fire was signed. So instead of "nothing," we should have the word "attack."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have reached the end of our session. We will meet again at 9.00 tomorrow, and I would like to point out to the Prosecutor that there is still an hour and 35 minutes left. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 27th day of January, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
